initial_observation.demographics: A 5-year-old girl born to noncontagious parents, after an uneventful pregnancy
initial_observation.encounter_context: First clinical encounter because of a transverse cutaneous “split” on the plantar aspect of the right third toe present for 3 months with serous discharge
initial_observation.chief_complaint: Transverse cutaneous “split” on the plantar aspect of the right third toe
initial_observation.first_contact_summary: The patient presented with a transverse cutaneous “split” on the plantar aspect of the right third toe of 3 months duration associated with serous discharge that gradually elongated circumferentially to involve the dorsal aspect within 1 month. She had no history of traveling, Raynaud phenomenon, trauma, exposure to vinyl chloride gas, skin fragility, blisters, joint pain, or swelling. No family history of similar lesions. Examination showed a distinct skin boundary ('split' sign) on the third toe and shortening of the distal phalanx of the second, fourth, and fifth toes. Sensation and pulses were normal.
presenting_symptoms: Transverse cutaneous “split” on the plantar aspect of the right third toe for 3 months
Elongation of the split circumferentially over 1 month
Shortening of distal phalanx of the 2nd, 4th, and 5th toes
known_prior_history: Mother reported similar demarcation line on the 2nd, 4th, and 5th toes of right foot with durations of 3 months, 1 year, and 2 years that disappeared before shortening of those toes
No history of traveling, Raynaud phenomenon, trauma, exposure to vinyl chloride gas, skin fragility, blisters, joint pain, or swelling
No family members with similar lesions

evidence_items.source_text: Examination of the feet revealed a distinct boundary between normal skin and affected crusted skin overlying osteolysis (“split” sign) on the third toe involving circumferentially the entire toe (Fig. 1). It was slightly painful and associated with serous discharge but no discharge of the bony spicules. Additionally, there was a shortening of the distal phalanx of the second, fourth, and fifth toes. The sensation and peripheral pulses of the feet were normal.

X-rays of the right foot revealed complete resorption of the middle and terminal phalanx of the fifth toe, complete resorption of the terminal phalanx of the fourth toe, partial resorption of the terminal phalanx of the third toe, and partial resorption of the middle and terminal phalanx of the second toe (Fig. 2).

Laboratory investigations that included complete blood count, renal function tests, liver function tests, parathyroid hormone, anti-nuclear antibody, rheumatoid factor, anti-CCP test, C-reactive protein, fasting blood sugar, serum calcium, inorganic phosphate, albumin, and thyroid function tests were in normal ranges. This workup helped rule out infections, e.g., osteomyelitis, connective tissue, endocrine, and lipid storage disease. There were no clinical or radiographic findings of inflammatory/rheumatic disorders such as psoriatic arthritis.
The clinical and radiologic features and workup helped establish the diagnosis of IAO in our patient.
